subject: PSHE
title: Rights responsibilities and our community
outcome: Explore rights, responsibilities and getting on as citizens.
credit: Lesson resource · CC BY-NC-SA 4.0: free for classroom use, share and adapt with credit, no resale
definition: A right is a basic thing everyone is entitled to. Rights are not prizes for good behaviour. A responsibility is a way to act with care for others and help protect their rights. A person still has rights if they break a rule. Adults help with fair and safe ways to put things right.
citizenship: In this lesson, getting on as citizens means taking part and caring for a shared community. Everyone can contribute. It is not a test of a person's background or legal status. A fair rule considers people's needs and access. Fair does not always mean that everyone gets the same help or time.

pairs.right: Everyone has a right to be heard.
pairs.responsibility: Listen and let others have a turn to give a view.
pairs.reason: Each view matters. Being heard does not mean getting every choice.

pairs.right: Everyone has a right to learn and take part.
pairs.responsibility: Help keep shared tasks and routes open to others.
pairs.reason: People may need different support or more space to join in.

pairs.right: Everyone has a right to safety.
pairs.responsibility: Use shared things with care and tell a trusted adult about a concern.
pairs.reason: Adults help keep people safe. A concern does not need proof first.

pairs.right: Everyone has a right to privacy.
pairs.responsibility: Ask before sharing another person's work or details.
pairs.reason: Privacy does not mean keeping a safety concern secret. Staff share concerns with the safeguarding lead.

pair_rule: Match each right to an action that helps protect it. Several actions may protect more than one right; explain the link. Rights are not earned by doing the action. Adults also have duties to protect rights. Do not make rights depend on obedience or take them away as a punishment.

case.title: A shared activity space
case.text: In a made-up community activity, young people share a table for card models. A stack of boxes narrows the route to the table. One learner needs a clear route for their usual access aid. Another learner keeps choosing each task without asking the group. The group wants a fair way for everyone to join in. No real people or places are used.
case.model: Everyone keeps their rights to take part, be heard and be safe. The group can ask the adult activity leader to make the route clear safely. They can listen to each view and agree a fair plan for turns, with any access support needed. They must not move another person's aid or belongings without asking. If the plan is not safe or fair, tell a trusted adult.
case.safer_step: Ask the adult activity leader for a clear route, then hear each view and agree supported turns. Rights stay in place while adults help with any rule problem.

charter.instruction: Draft three short lines for an invented class. Each line links a right to an action that helps protect it. Keep everyone's rights in place, allow access needs and include a trusted adult help route. This is an imagined charter, not a rule or contract for the real group. No names or signatures.
model: Everyone can have a say. We listen in each person's usual way.
Everyone can take part. We make space and use fair turns with support.
Everyone can be safe. We use things with care and ask a trusted adult for help.
charter.voice: A learner may suggest a change through words, pointing, typing or an aid, or pass. A staff listener records the fictional charter idea and explains how it could improve the draft. A vote or loud voice cannot remove another person's rights. No agreement to real rules or public speaking is required.

choices.B: Make a map with right and action pairs, three charter lines, then a safe and fair step for the community scene with a reason and help route.
choices.C: Write a short community advice note with right and action pairs, three charter lines, then a safe and fair step for the same scene with a reason and help route.

success: Link a right to an action that helps protect it, without making the right a reward.
Draft three fair charter lines for an invented class, including access and help.
Use the invented community scene to explain a fair step and trusted adult help.
private_card: All charter and scene work is fictional. No personal background, real dispute, name or signature is requested. Optional personal reminders stay with the pupil and are not collected, photographed, displayed or compared. Blank, pass and a supervised pause remain valid. No learner must sign or agree to a real class charter.
help: Ask a trusted adult or school staff in private. Use words, a note, HELP or a usual aid. Staff can take a concern to the safeguarding lead through school procedure. If one adult is unavailable or help is not enough, ask another trusted adult. For an immediate safety concern, get adult help at once. No named service, organisation, website or phone number is needed.
step_out: Before teaching, agree the discreet HELP or PAUSE signal and familiar supervised place and route. Staff acknowledge it quietly and keep adult support. No public reason is needed. Offer a neutral task, supported return or private catch-up. Do not send a learner away alone. Pass is not failure.
safeguarding: Any disclosure goes to the safeguarding lead through school procedure. Listen calmly, reassure, do not probe, investigate or promise secrecy. Follow urgent school procedures for immediate concerns. Keep real concerns and identifying details in the separate safeguarding record, not learning evidence. A pupil unable to identify a trusted adult is supported privately, not pressed.

routes.Supported: Choose either format and complete all parts. Use the short right and action choices, word bank, starter and visible model. Point, type, use a usual aid or exact scribe with readback. Separate content cues from usual access.
routes.Independent: Choose either format. Link rights and actions with reasons, draft three fair charter lines and apply them to the scene with help. Keep the model and usual aids. No real community experience is needed.
routes.Aspire: Choose either format and complete all parts. Explain why rights cannot be earned or removed. Check a charter line for access and privacy limits, then adapt the community plan if the first suggestion does not work. No extra personal detail is required.

scaffolds.model: Everyone has a right to be heard.
Listening helps protect a right to be heard.
Ask the adult leader for a clear route.
Rights belong to everyone, even when a rule is broken.
Everyone can take part. We make space with help.

scaffolds.start: One change to the draft is…
scaffolds.model: Allow each person's usual way to give a view.

scaffolds.start: If the plan is not fair…
scaffolds.model: Ask a trusted adult for help to put it right.

hinge.question: A learner breaks a turn rule. What happens to their rights?
choices: A They lose every right until they behave.
B Their rights stay. Adults help with a fair and safe next step.
C The loudest person can take their rights away.
D The group must hide every concern for privacy.
hinge.parallel: A group agrees a plan that blocks a learner's access. A Ask an adult to adapt it fairly. B Keep it because a vote can remove rights.
hinge.rule: Check privately. B or safe equivalent with a reason: proceed. A makes rights a reward; C treats power as permission; D confuses privacy with secrecy. Re-model with the invented scene, then use parallel A. Pass or no response is unobserved; revisit with support, not a failure label.

timing: Settle, agree help and pause; choose a right or explain its link to care.
Teach rights and responsibilities. Rights stay with everyone; match four right and action pairs.
Model the invented community scene and one charter line. Match a step or improve advice.
Check rights are not a reward. Choose map or note and usual response mode.
One format covering pairs, three charter lines and the community response; include pupil voice about the fictional draft.
Use shared checks; staff listener gives one next step and retains the pupil response.
Explain a right and helpful action, or repair a rights myth. Confirm help.
where_this_leads: This helps me contribute to a group, respect rights and ask for fair support in learning and future work.
marking: Retain actual fictional learning evidence, usual access and content prompts. Set one NS and allow a reply in the same colour, on the same page or usual mode. E only for actual saved work. R only after Voice, Audience, one NS and an actual pupil response. Offer to the Communication portfolio; staff confirm any mapping. Optional personal reminders and real concerns are not learning evidence. Any offer for the unit award depends on staff checking actual evidence and current requirements.

paragraphs: Explore rights, responsibilities and getting on as citizens.

A right is a basic thing everyone is entitled to. Rights are not prizes for good behaviour. A responsibility is a way to act with care for others and help protect their rights. A person still has rights if they break a rule. Adults help with fair and safe ways to put things right.

In this lesson, getting on as citizens means taking part and caring for a shared community. Everyone can contribute. It is not a test of a person's background or legal status. A fair rule considers people's needs and access. Fair does not always mean that everyone gets the same help or time.

Match each right to an action that helps protect it. Several actions may protect more than one right; explain the link. Rights are not earned by doing the action. Adults also have duties to protect rights. Do not make rights depend on obedience or take them away as a punishment.

Suggested matches are 1 B, 2 D, 3 A and 4 C. Several actions can help protect more than one right. Accept another safe link with a clear explanation. The action never earns the right. Adults also have duties to protect rights.

Draft three short lines for an invented class. Each line links a right to an action that helps protect it. Keep everyone's rights in place, allow access needs and include a trusted adult help route. This is an imagined charter, not a rule or contract for the real group. No names or signatures.
Everyone can have a say. We listen in each person's usual way.
Everyone can take part. We make space and use fair turns with support.
Everyone can be safe. We use things with care and ask a trusted adult for help.

Everyone keeps their rights to take part, be heard and be safe. The group can ask the adult activity leader to make the route clear safely. They can listen to each view and agree a fair plan for turns, with any access support needed. They must not move another person's aid or belongings without asking. If the plan is not safe or fair, tell a trusted adult.

Map B and note C both include all four matches and a reason, three charter lines, and the community step, reason and help. A map needs no art skill and a note needs no extra length. Keep models and usual aids available while recording actual content help.

Main B. A makes rights a reward. C treats power as permission. D confuses privacy with secrecy. Re-model then use parallel A: ask an adult to adapt the plan fairly. A pass is unobserved. Check privately in the usual response mode.

Basic rights stay when a rule is broken. Responsibilities help protect rights rather than buy them. Fair support can differ because needs differ. Being heard does not mean always getting a choice. Privacy has safeguarding limits; a safety concern is shared with the safeguarding lead through school procedure.

Check the three task parts and reasons from fictional work. Retain partial evidence and actual prompts. Usual aids, typing and exact scribing do not supply answers. Log adult answer choices or models as content help. Do not judge real conduct, personal background, legal status or agreement to real class rules.

A learner may suggest a change through words, pointing, typing or an aid, or pass. A staff listener records the fictional charter idea and explains how it could improve the draft. A vote or loud voice cannot remove another person's rights. No agreement to real rules or public speaking is required.

Use printed pairs, the made-up class and community scene if display fails. No real signatures, access-route changes, moving aids, live accounts or personal disputes. Adults organise safe access. For any actual concern use the school help and safeguarding routes.

Optional personal reminders and real concerns are not learning evidence. Any offer for the unit award depends on staff checking actual evidence and current requirements.

Ask a trusted adult or school staff in private. Use words, a note, HELP or a usual aid. Staff can take a concern to the safeguarding lead through school procedure. If one adult is unavailable or help is not enough, ask another trusted adult. For an immediate safety concern, get adult help at once. No named service, organisation, website or phone number is needed.

An action helps protect a right. It does not earn it. Rights are not prizes for good behaviour. A person still has rights if a rule is broken. Adults help with fair and safe next steps.
Some actions may help more than one right. Explain the link. Privacy does not mean keeping a safety concern secret; school staff share it with the safeguarding lead.

Everyone can be safe. We use things with care and ask a trusted adult for help.

Use words, pointing, typing, a note or a usual aid, or pass. The staff listener hears your fictional charter idea and explains how it could help the draft. You do not have to speak to the group or agree to real class rules.

In a made-up community activity, young people share a table for card models. A stack of boxes narrows the route to the table. One learner needs a clear route for their usual access aid. Another learner keeps choosing each task without asking the group. The group wants a fair way for everyone to join in. No real people or places are used.

If the plan is not safe or fair, tell a trusted adult.
Give a safe and fair step, a reason and trusted adult help. The adult leader can make the route clear safely. Do not move any aid or belongings without asking.

Write a short community advice note with right and action pairs, three charter lines, then a safe and fair step for the same scene with a reason and help route.

paragraphs: Use these words with the invented class and community scene. No personal background, real dispute or legal status is needed.
A basic thing everyone is entitled to. Rights are not prizes for good behaviour.
A way to act with care for others and help protect rights. Doing it does not earn a right.
People who share a place, group or activity. Everyone can contribute.
A short shared plan about how a group aims to act. This lesson uses an invented class, not a real contract.
Respect rights and needs. Different people may need different help or time.
Care with personal details. A safety concern is shared with people who can help, including the safeguarding lead.

Can we talk in private? I would like help.
If one adult is busy or help is not enough, ask another trusted adult.
Everyone has a right to be heard. Listening helps protect that right. A person still has rights if they break a turn rule. Adults help put things right fairly.
Point, use an aid, type or ask for an exact scribe. The adult reads back quietly so you can correct it. You may pass or use the agreed supported pause.

Total 40 minutes. Processing time and short quiet pauses sit inside these phases. Both formats include the same three parts within one task period. Reuse the four matches from guided work; do not add a second matching task.
Where this leads: This helps me contribute to a group, respect rights and ask for fair support in learning and future work.
Choose a right from the cards. Or explain how listening can help another person take part. Use the invented group only.

A right belongs to everyone. It is not a prize for good behaviour. Responsibilities help protect rights. Rights stay if a rule is broken. Adults help with a safe, fair response. Getting on as citizens here means caring for a shared community; no personal background or legal status is tested.

Everyone keeps their rights. Ask the adult leader to clear the route safely. Hear each view and agree fair turns with access support. Do not move an aid or belongings without asking. Tell a trusted adult if the plan is unsafe or unfair.

Explain why rights are not earned. Check access and privacy limits, then adapt the community plan if the first suggestion does not work.

Books are the first route. Evidence Sheet page 2 offers Type instead for both formats. Point, draw, use a usual aid or exact scribe. Read back quietly and allow correction. Keep reading and language aids. Plan in any language. No public questioning.

Point to the place or instruction. Ask a short private question. Rephrase. Offer a scaffold or choice. Model the first step only, then return the task. Allow time. Record answer cues apart from usual access.

A learner breaks a turn rule. What happens to their rights? A They lose every right until they behave. B Their rights stay. Adults help with a fair and safe next step. C The loudest person can take their rights away. D The group must hide every concern for privacy. Check privately. B or safe equivalent with a reason: proceed. A makes rights a reward; C treats power as permission; D confuses privacy with secrecy. Re-model with the invented scene, then use parallel A. Pass or no response is unobserved; revisit with support, not a failure label.

A group agrees a plan that blocks a learner's access. A Ask an adult to adapt it fairly. B Keep it because a vote can remove rights. Correct A. A plan must respect access and rights. A pass is unobserved.

F Which right could listening help protect? M Why may different support be fair? H Why can a vote not remove a right or hide a safety concern? Use words, a note, pointing or a usual aid. No public questioning.

Rights are not earned by obedience or removed as a punishment. Responsibilities help protect rights, not buy them. Fairness considers needs; it does not always mean the same help or time. Privacy is not secrecy about safety. A view can be heard without every wish being agreed.

Cognition and Learning: one part at a time, visible model and short choices. Communication and Interaction: wait time, aid, typing or exact scribe with quiet readback. SEMH: predictable mild scene, private response, pass, neutral task and supervised pause. Sensory and Physical: clear print, comfortable position and usual aids; discuss access without asking about personal needs. EAL: explain key words and plan in any language.

Input: model a right and action link. Guided work: offer a match or advice repair. Independent: check all three parts privately, record actual aids and answer cues, acknowledge pause signals and keep supervision. Do not supply missing answers or ask for real class disputes.

A learner may suggest a change through words, pointing, typing or an aid, or pass. A staff listener records the fictional charter idea and explains how it could improve the draft. A vote or loud voice cannot remove another person's rights. No agreement to real rules or public speaking is required.

Use fictional work only. Check all four matches and a reason, the three charter lines, then the community step, reason and help route. Keep partial work and actual prompts. A pass is unobserved. Learning work does not prove conduct in a real community. No signature or personal agreement is evidence.

Use shared checks or improve A right is a reward. Set one precise NS and retain the reply. Exit: give a right and helpful action or correct A vote can remove a right. The learning self-check is Ready to explain / With a prompt / Need another example. It does not rate a person, background or behaviour.

Optional personal reminders and real concerns are not learning evidence. Any offer for the unit award depends on staff checking actual evidence and current requirements.

Do not move an aid, rearrange real access routes, sign an actual charter or stage a real dispute. The adult activity leader makes the fictional route clear safely. Follow school procedures for any actual concern.

No named service, organisation, website or phone number is needed.
